headline: Shinu has an irregular -nu ending shared only with the now-obsolete verb 往ぬ (inu).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *sin-. Appears in the oldest Japanese texts, including the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE and the Man'yōshū of 759 CE.

The ぬ (-nu) ending historically had an irregular conjugation pattern, shared only by now-obsolete verb 往(い)ぬ, 去(い)ぬ (inu, “to go away, to go, to leave, to pass, to disappear”) and auxiliary verb ぬ (nu, indicating completion, generally reserved for non-intentional, spontaneous, or intransitive actions). The ぬ (-nu) in verb 死(し)ぬ (shinu) was viewed as identical to the auxiliary, and the verb 死(し)ぬ (shinu) initially was thus never conjugated with this auxiliary as an additional suffix.

The auxiliary itself may have derived from the verb 往(い)ぬ, 去(い)ぬ (inu, “to go away, to go, to leave, to pass, to disappear”), raising the possibility that the verb 死(し)ぬ (shinu) may have derived from a fusion of 死(し) (shi, “death”) + 往(い)ぬ, 去(い)ぬ (inu, “to go away, to go, to leave, to pass, to disappear”); the second element could also be the auxiliary ぬ (-nu) or its suggested ancient stative verb origin.

The transition from the ナ行(ぎょう)変(へん)格(かく)活(かつ)用(よう) (na-gyō henkaku katsuyō, “na-row irregular conjugation”) pattern to the regular 四(よ)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (yodan katsuyō, “quadrigrade conjugation”) appears in texts from the Muromachi period (1336–1573) and on. The na irregular pattern persisted in increasingly limited use until the Meiji period (1868–1929).

headline: Yasashii is cognate with 優しい (yasashii).

sources.quote: Cognate with 優(やさ)しい (yasashii).

headline: Otōsan began as o- plus 父 (toto) plus 様 (-sama); the long ō was an artificial step.

sources.quote: Originally a compound of 御(お) (o-, “honorific prefix”) + 父(とと) (toto, “father”) + 様(さま) (-sama, “honorific suffix”).
/ototosama/ → /otottsan/ → /otossan/

The /otossan/ → /otoosan/ progression was artificial; regular Japanese sound changes generally would not allow this shift. The /otoosan/ form first appears in the early Meiji period in educational materials mandated by the 文部省 (Monbushō, “Ministry of Education”).

examples.ja: おとうさんには言わないでね。
彼がおとうさんの代わりにその会合に出ました。
examples.en: He attended the meeting for his father.

headline: Odoru was wodoru, and its original meaning was “to jump”.

sources.quote: * ⟨wodo₂ru⟩ → */wodəru/ → /wodoru/ → /odoru/
From Old Japanese, with the original meaning of "to jump". First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE. From Proto-Japonic *wontəru.

sources.quote: Attested in the late Heian period. Possibly cognate with 嘯(うそぶ)く (usobuku, “to boast”) and 似非(えせ) (ese, “fake, false”).

sources.quote: /rjokau/ → /rjokɔː/ → /rjokoː/
From Middle Chinese compound 旅行 (ljo^X hæng, literally “to travel + to walk”). Compare modern Hakka reading lî-hàng, Min Nan readings lí-hêng, lú-hêng.

headline: Iriguchi is 入り + 口, and kuchi changes to guchi by rendaku.

sources.quote: Compound of 入り (iri, “entry, going in”) + 口 (kuchi, “mouth; opening”). The kuchi changes to guchi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

meaning: to become cloudy, to become dim
headline: Kumoru is the noun 雲 (kumo, “cloud”) plus the verb suffix る (-ru): cloud, made into a verb.

sources.quote: From the noun 雲(くも) (kumo, “cloud”) + る (-ru, verb suffix).

headline: Atama has an unknown derivation, with theories like heaven (a) plus ball (tama).

sources.quote: Probably from Old Japanese. First cited in the ten-volume Wamyō Ruijushō of 934 CE.
Unknown derivation. Theories include:
* Compound of 天(あ) (a, “heaven, sky”) + 玉(たま) (tama, “ball”). This is problematic phonetically, as 天 appears historically as ama or ame, not as just a.

* Compound of 当(あ)て (ate, “putting something in contact”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 当(あ)てる (ateru, “to hit”)) + 間(ま) (ma, “space, gap”), referring to the head as a moxibustion point. This is also problematic phonetically, as the shift from ate to ata necessitates a change in meaning of the underlying verb. This is also problematic semantically, as the term 間(ま) (ma) term refers more specifically to a gap or space.

* Compound of 貴(あて) (ate, “noble”) + 間(ま) (ma, “space”), referring to the most important part of the body. However, the use of 間(ま) (ma) in this way is again problematic. Moreover, 貴(あて) (ate, “noble”) appears in The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter dating to the 900s CE, while 頭(あたま) (atama) with a sense of fontanelle appears in the Wamyō Ruijushō dated 938 CE, leaving insufficient time for either the semantic or phonetic drift required.

Historically, this term first appears with a sense of fontanelle, in reference to the soft place on the top of an infant's head where the bones of the skull have not yet fused. As such, a more likely derivation might be as a compound of 当(あ)た (ata, “not quite touching, not quite in contact”, 未(み)然(ぜん)形(けい) (mizenkei, “irrealis form”) of classical verb 当(あ)つ (atsu) and root of modern 当(あ)たる (ataru, “to touch, to come into contact”)) + 間(ま) (ma, “space, gap, opening”).

headline: Han is from Middle Chinese 半 (MC panH).

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 半 (MC panH).

examples.en: I bought half a dozen eggs.

examples.ja: 海までわずか半マイルだ。
examples.en: It is no more than half a mile to the sea.

headline: Sukunai is possibly related to 少し (sukoshi), and possibly cognate with the ku in 幾 (iku).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Possibly related to 少し (sukoshi). Possibly cognate with the ku part in 幾 (iku).

headline: Warui is from classical わろし (waroshi); compare まるい (marui) from まろし (maroshi).

sources.quote: From classical わろし (waroshi). Compare まるい (marui) < まろし (maroshi).

headline: Ōkii went opoki → oɸoki → oɸokiki → owokiː → oːkiː, and appears in the Muromachi period.

sources.quote: /opoki/ → /oɸoki/ → /oɸokiki/ → /owokiː/ → /oːkiː/
Appears in the Muromachi period, 1337 to 1573 CE.

From older adjective 大(おお)き (ōki, ancient reading opoki), derived as the attributive form ōki (ancient opoki) of cognate adjective ōshi (ancient oposi; attributive opoki appearing already in the Man'yōshū of 759 CE, meaning both “large” or “many”, spelled as 多(おお)し (ōshi) or 大(おお)し (ōshi), modern Japanese 多(おお)い (ōi, “many”)), in turn derived from Old Japanese adjective opo (“indistinct; of uncertain size, shape, or amount”; read as ō in modern Japanese, spelled as 凡 or 大).

meaning: to see, to look at, to watch
headline: Miru is cognate with 目 (me, “eye”) and first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. From Proto-Japonic *miru. Cognate with 目(め) (me, “eye”).

headline: Ten is from Middle Chinese 點 (MC temX, “point”).

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 點 (MC temX, “point”).

headline: Shichi is from Middle Chinese 七 (MC tshit).

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 七 (MC tshit). Compare Hokkien 七 (chhit), Hakka 七 (chhit).

examples.ja: 彼女は七時に駅に着いた。
examples.en: She got to the station at seven.

examples.ja: 今夜七時に、電話するよ。
examples.en: I'll ring you up at seven this evening.

headline: Semai was originally sebashi, before it became semashi and then lost its medial k.

sources.quote: From Early Middle Japanese adjective 狭(せま)し (semashi), with the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “predicative form”) ending in し (shi) first replaced with the 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) ending in き (ki), and then with the medial /-k-/ falling out to result in an ending of い (i). Originally 狭し (sebashi); underwent a sound change from /b/ to /m/, similar to 寂しい (sabishii, samishii, “lonely, desolate”), 頭 (tsuburi, tsumuri, “head”), and 煙 (keburi, kemuri, “smoke”).
Cognate with 攻(せ)める (semeru), 責(せ)める (semeru), 迫(せま)る (semaru), 狭(せば)める (sebameru), and 狭(せば)まる (sebamaru), and 窄(すば)る (subaru, “to become narrow”).

headline: Mizu is possibly cognate with 瑞 (mizu, “freshness, youth”).

sources.quote: ⟨mi₁du⟩ → */mʲidu/ → /mid͡zu/ → /mizu/
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. In turn, from Proto-Japonic *mentu. Ryukyuan cognates support the existence of the first vowel having an initial mid vowel.
Possibly cognate with 瑞 (mizu, “freshness, youth”).

examples.en: Like water off a duck's back.

headline: Dōbutsu is from Middle Chinese 動物.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 動物 (duwng^X mjut)

examples.en: A dragon is a creature of fancy.

headline: Shitsurei is literally “lose, loss + propriety”, probably from Middle Chinese 失禮.

sources.quote: Probably from Middle Chinese compound 失禮 /失礼 (syit lej^X, literally “lose, loss + propriety”). Compare modern Hokkien 失禮 /失礼 (sit-lé).

examples.ja: こんな格好でしつれいします。
examples.en: Pardon me for being in this dress.

headline: Mainichi is 毎 (mai-, “each; every”) plus 日 (nichi, jitsu, “day”).

sources.quote: 毎 (mai-, “each; every”) + 日 (nichi, jitsu, “day”)

headline: Oya may be cognate with the verb 老ゆ (oyu, “to become old”), from the idea of one's elders.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *oya. Cognate with or derived from Old Japanese verb 老ゆ (oyu, “to become old”, modern 老いる oiru), from the idea of one's elders.
First cited in the Kojiki of 712.

examples.en: It is a wise father that knows his own child.

headline: Toshi originally referred to grain, particularly rice, and by extension the year's harvest.

sources.quote: ⟨to₂si⟩ → /tosi/ → /toɕi/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *təsi. Originally referred to grain, particularly rice, and by extension, the year's harvest.

headline: Yasui first appears in the Kojiki spelled 夜須 (yasu), and is cognate with 休む (yasumu, “to rest”).

sources.quote: From classical 安(やす)し (yasushi), from Old Japanese. First appears in the Kojiki of 712 CE as 夜須（久） (yasu(ku)). In turn from Proto-Japonic *yasu. Cognate with 休(やす)む (yasumu, “to rest”).

headline: Yowai was 弱し in Old Japanese, and a king's name varies between 目弱王 and 眉輪王.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 弱し (*yo₁wasi), from Proto-Japonic *yowa-.
Although not phonetically attested in Old Japanese texts in man'yōgana, the name of a king varies between 目弱王 in the Kojiki and 眉輪王, read as mayo₁wa-WAU in the Nihon Shoki.

headline: Shiro is the standalone apophonic form of shira, from Proto-Japonic *siro.

sources.quote: ⟨siro₁⟩ → */sirʷo/ → /ɕiro/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *siro.
The standalone apophonic form of shira below.

headline: Mono is attested in the Kojiki, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *mənə.

sources.quote: ⟨mo₂no₂⟩ → ⟨mono₂⟩ → /mono/
From Old Japanese. Attested in the Kojiki. Ultimately from Proto-Japonic *mənə.

examples.en: I don't have a thing to wear.

headline: Akanbō is attested from the 19th century, shifted from earlier 赤坊 (akabō): 赤 (aka, “red”) plus 坊 (-bō, “little”).

sources.quote: Attested from the 19th century. Sound shift from slightly earlier 赤坊 (akabō), from 赤 (aka, “red”) + 坊 (-bō, “little”). Compare 赤ちゃん (aka-chan) and 赤子 (akago), both of which also allude to the reddish complexion of a newborn.

meaning: very hard (as in "to work hard"), with utmost effort
headline: Isshōkenmei comes from 一所懸命 (isshokenmei), which referred to samurai risking their life to defend inherited territory.

sources.quote: Yojijukugo (四(よ)字(じ)熟(じゅく)語(ご)), from 一所懸命(いっしょけんめい) (isshokenmei), which referred to samurais risking their life to defend the territory inherited from ancestors.

examples.en: I ran as fast as I could.

meaning: to put (things) side by side; to line up
headline: Naraberu is the lower monograde shift of 並ぶ (narabu), attested as early as the Man'yōshū of 759 CE.

sources.quote: The regular 下一段活用 (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) shift of Old Japanese and Classical Japanese verb 並ぶ (narabu, “to line up (intransitive); to line something up (transitive)”).
The root verb narabu appears in Old Japanese, at least as early as the Man'yōshū of 759 CE.

Probably reflecting the same nara root as verb 均す・平す (narasu, “to flatten something out, to line something up horizontally”) + ぶ (bu, suffix attaching to nouns and adjectives to indicate ongoing state or likeness). If so, probably deriving ultimately from verb 成る・為る・生る (naru, “to come into being; to become”), 慣る・馴る・狎る・熟る (naru, “to become normal, to become regular, to become fitting”, classical form of modern なれる (nareru)).

examples.ja: 彼は肩をならべていた。
examples.en: He was standing shoulder to shoulder.

examples.ja: 大きさ順に本を並べた。
examples.en: We arranged the books according to size.
